strengths: The paper is well-written and easy to follow in most parts. Moreover, the work is well-motivated and I enjoyed that the authors brought back old ideas to the BDL community, e.g., using the discriminant analysis as a likelihood model.

I believe the exposition of the method is well done in most places, though slightly dense here and there, and helped in understanding the general idea of the proposed method. Moreover, I believe that the method is correct and an interesting contribution to the field. I think it is important to see more work on deterministic approaches to uncertainty quantification in deep learning.
The experimental section shows promising results, especially in the case of regression.
BLL networks are an interesting approach to solve the scalability problem Bayesian neural networks tend to suffer from.
The paper introduces another variation to this family of approaches that is relatively straightforward, easy to understand, and implement.
The method is properly evaluated as the number of experimental setups is reasonably extensive both with respect to architectures and experimental tasks.

This is an excellent paper and a significant contribution - well done! The authors make clear how they build on the existing literature in Bayesian deep learning to create a novel advance that is practical and easy to implement. This is significant and should enable more work to push the frontier of the "best of both worlds", with neural networks serving as function approximators and Bayesian methods enabling sample-efficiency and quantification of uncertainty that is required for practical deployment of deep learning.
I found the paper very interesting and easy to read. Uncertainty estimation is an important and active research area in deep learning.
To the best of my knowledge, the idea is novel (although not groundbreaking)
The method is scalable, simple to implement in standard architectures, and achieves very competitive performances (especially considering its simplicity)

While being Bayesian only on the last neural network layer the method is in principle not as powerful as other techniques, as the authors rightly claim simpler methods that are easy to implement are what is being more commonly used in practice (e.g., Bayesian dropout, stochastic weight averaging)
The appendix is extensive and addresses all the details I felt were missing in the main paper
weaknesses: My main concern with the paper is the weak empirical evaluation and limited novelty of the work, that is, it seems it is essentially an application of known techniques to the special case of last-layer posteriors.

Section 2.4 lists various related works, which I believe the author claims to optimize the log marginal via gradient descent. It appears that this statement is false for at least a subset of the cited papers. It might be good to revise the exposition.

Eq 12 is some weighted ELBO, weighted with T for the purpose of generality, however T never seems to be used later and makes the connection to the common ELBO less transparent. The paper would improve in clarity if T is dropped.
Section 3.4 is very dense and it could help the reader if this section is improved in its presentation.

For the experiments, I would have expected assessments under distributional shift, a comparison to recent deterministic approaches (e.g., Zeng et al 2023 or Dhawan et al 2023), and a large-scale application of the approach as it acts on the last-layer only and should be applicable in more realistic scenarios (e.g., ImageNet).

Straight‑forward contributions can be a weakness if they do not provide a clear theoretical benefit above current approaches and also come without clear performance improvements; the results are rather mixed despite strong wordings.
The abstract and contributions promise improved predictive accuracy, calibration, and OOD detection, and claim extremely strong performance, which is not supported by the actual results.
The presentation of regression experiments is unclear, e.g., what does a bold number mean?
The method improves on only two of six UCI data sets, is slightly better on one, equal on two, and worse on one, making the claim of strong performance misleading.
All baselines are simply cited from prior work; variations in train/test splits and unspecified error intervals raise concerns about the trustworthiness of the results.
Potential differences in data normalization compared to cited results are acknowledged, but it is unclear how they affect the results.
Classification results are at best comparable to competitive baselines despite claims of extremely strong accuracy, ECE, NLL, and OOD detection.
The method is simpler than baselines but lacks a convincing argument for why this should matter, and no runtime comparisons are provided to support the claim of practical benefits.

Visualizations of how tight or loose the bounds in the main text could help build more intuition; comparisons in terms of speed or efficiency to variational inference algorithms that require sampling could also help guide practitioners.

To increase the impact of the paper, code should be made publicly available and good default hyperparameters should be set, especially to help those not familiar with VI implement the mixed parameterization.
Drawing graphical models of the models presented in Section 2 would help the reader visualize the random variables and their (hyper)priors/parameters.
Details on the generative classification model could be moved to the appendix, especially given the poorer performances.
